name: Collecting Emissions Data
title: Collecting Emissions Data
answer: Collecting emissions data is the practice of gathering the activity and quantity figures that carbon accounting turns into a footprint. It covers the fuels, electricity, travel, freight, materials and waste that an organisation consumes or produces, plus the emission factors that convert those quantities into carbon dioxide equivalent. The scope spans everything from a single site's utility bills to a group's worldwide operations, and it is the input stage on which every later calculation, report and assurance opinion depends.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data is the practice of gathering the activity and quantity figures that carbon accounting turns into a footprint. It covers the fuels, electricity, travel, freight, materials and waste that an organisation consumes or produces, plus the emission factors that convert those quantities into carbon dioxide equivalent. The scope spans everything from a single site's utility bills to a group's worldwide operations, and it is the input stage on which every later calculation, report and assurance opinion depends.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of source systems and the tools that connect them. Meter readings, invoices, fuel cards, expense claims, purchase orders, fleet logs and building management systems hold the raw activity data, while spreadsheets, ERP modules and dedicated carbon platforms hold the factors and the calculations. Emission factor sets such as those published by government bodies or maintained by standards organisations supply the conversion values, and the whole chain depends on consistent units, periods and boundaries.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by setting the organisational and operational boundary, then map each emission source to a data owner and a collection route. Activity data is pulled from invoices, meters and systems, checked for gaps and duplicates, and multiplied by a matching emission factor. Estimates fill what cannot be measured directly, and the results are reviewed against prior periods before they are consolidated. The method is closer to careful bookkeeping than to modelling, and its quality rests on documentation, traceability and consistent treatment year on year.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk sit around who owns the data, how it may be used and how far it can be trusted. Supplier data may arrive under confidentiality terms, personal travel and payroll records attract privacy duties, and estimates must be labelled as such rather than presented as measured fact. Provenance matters because auditors and regulators need to trace a reported figure back to its source document and factor version. Weak controls invite greenwashing claims, restatements and penalties, so version control, sign off and a clear audit trail are part of the collection process itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Collection is moving from annual spreadsheet exercises toward continuous, system to system flows. Smart meters, telematics, procurement platforms and utility APIs can feed activity data automatically, and standardised digital formats make that data easier to exchange and verify. The pressure is toward finer granularity, clearer provenance and tighter links between reported figures and their evidence. The open questions are how to keep estimates honest, how to handle supplier data at scale, and how to make all of it auditable without slowing the business down.
